name: Bau-Jagoi Bidayuh
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bau-Jagoi Bidayuh (baub1235) is not in the catalog. The two bibliography items are one work: Rensch, 'Rhythm in Bidayuh', 10-ICAL 2006 preprint = SPLC 19:84-91 (2008). The 2006 PDF (and its abstract) were fetched sources open from sil-philippines-languages.org (the Glottolog URL's redirect target) and with and md5s; the SPLC print copy itself was not located (sil.org blocks fetches, no Wayback capture) but is the same paper. The paper is chiefly about vowel-duration rhythm (lengthened ultima vowels; full vs reduced penult vowels, absent in Western dialects), and it states word stress directly: 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation' (§2, p. 2), with a Western-specific note that rearticulated V.V sequences carry the stress onset on the final vowel (fn 3). The fuller first-hand statement is Rensch et al. 2012 (SIL e-Book 33, already on file from the buka1257 sweep), §4.1.2 p. 47 and §3.3.2 p. 39, which names the western dialects (Singai, Jagoi) and says the ultima is the tonic syllable receiving the word accent, (C)V1.ˈV1(C); fn 79 p. 94 and §6.2.4 p. 292 repeat final stress (citation forms; utterance-final). Reading: fixed final word stress, non-contrastive, no length/tone in Western Bidayuh; a catalog record for baub1235 could be built on these two Rensch sources. Nothing remains to acquire (priority none for both items).

new_statements.quote: In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually). [...] In some words of the shape (C)V.V(C), in western dialects (Singai, Jagoi) and also in Rara, the same vowel occurs in both the ultima (last syllable) and the penult (second-to-last syllable). In such words initiation of stress (accent) on the ultima vowel is usually perceptible: (C)V1.ˈV1(C). [p. 47] || In western dialects words having the shape #(C)V1.V1(C)# are disyllabic. In such words #(C)V1 is the penult; V1(C)# is the ultima and as such is the tonic syllable. It receives the word-accent. [p. 39] || Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation. [Rensch 2006: 2]

new_statements.locator: Part II §4.1.2 'Structure of the ultima', p. 47 (PDF p. 64); Part II §3.3.2 'Rearticulated vowels', p. 39 (PDF p. 56); cf. p. 94 n. 79, p. 131, p. 292; Rensch 2006 §2, p. 2
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the last syllable (the ultima) of the word/stem in citation forms; this holds across the Bidayuh dialect network and is stated explicitly for the western (Singai, Jagoi = Bau-Jagoi) dialects, where even rearticulated same-vowel sequences (C)V1.V1(C) are two syllables with the accent on the final one. Stems are typically disyllabic; the penult never carries the peak.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any examined source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for placement. Word-final glides: stress 'falls on the first (more syllabic) of the two' vocoids, i.e. still the final syllable (p. 37). In Western (Bau-Jagoi) dialects rearticulated (C)V1.V1(C) words are disyllabic with the second (final) vowel stressed (p. 39, p. 47). The full/reduced penult-vowel contrast of eastern/central dialects does not operate in western dialects (p. 39; Rensch 2006 Pattern D), so no penult prominence contrast in Bau-Jagoi.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: 'at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually)' (p. 47); Rensch 2006 p. 2: 'at least in isolation'; Part III p. 292 adds that final-syllable accent is 'especially evident in utterance-final position'; p. 94 n.79: 'perhaps in context'. Post-clitics attached to a word take the stress (p. 94 n.79). No instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source treats 'Bidayuh' as a network of ~25 dialects in four clusters; Bau-Jagoi Bidayuh [sne] = Rensch's 'Western Bidayuh (Singai-Jagoi)' cluster (Singai, Jagoi, Serambu, Gumbang, Bratak, Krokong; Bau District). The p. 47 statement is pan-Bidayuh but is immediately followed by a western-dialect (Singai, Jagoi) specific stress remark, and §3.3.2 p. 39 is explicitly about western dialects; Rensch 2006 includes Serambu/Singai/Gumbang data. Not a description of one village dialect. Hliboi (Smith 2021, West Kalimantan) is only tentatively assigned to sne by Glottolog's bibliography.

new_statements.reading: Fixed final (ultima) word stress in all Bidayuh dialects, stated explicitly for the western (Singai, Jagoi = Bau-Jagoi) dialects: the ultima is the tonic syllable and carries the word accent, even when penult and ultima have the same vowel (CV1.ˈV1C); stress is non-contrastive; enclitics take the stress as the new final syllable; the 'at least in citation forms / especially utterance-final' hedge means connected-speech placement was not separately verified. Candidate catalog coding for baub1235: fixed final, domain WORD (citation forms), lexical_stress no, no phonemic length in Western Bidayuh (rearticulated vowels instead), no tone. Rensch 2006/2008 §2 p. 2 gives the same rule in one sentence and is the title-sweep source of record.

sources.quote: Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation. [...] In Western Bidayuh vowels may be rearticulated, i.e., there are sequences of identical (or diverse) vowels with the onset of the second vowel marked by an articulatory pulse coinciding with the onset of stress. For example, Gumbang (Western) [ . ] 'ironwood', [ . ] 'itchy'. These are sequences of vowels that form the nucleus of successive syllables. Western Bidayuh does not have lengthened vowels in the usual sense.
sources.locator: §2 'Rhythm differences', p. 2; fn 3, p. 3; Pattern D table, p. 5
sources.note: p. 2 §2: 'Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation.' Covers all four clusters incl. Western (Singai, Jagoi, Serambu, Gumbang data); fn. 3: Western rearticulated vowels have 'the onset of the second vowel marked by an articulatory pulse coinciding with the onset of stress'. Penult full/reduced contrast absent in Western dialects (Pattern D).
